rationale: Evidence from iteration 3 (score 395.7, the best so far). Reducing mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg raised the oval finish rate from 0.30 to 0.75 and cut oval max_error from about 0.055 to 0.035 m. That supports the hypothesis that lower yaw inertia helps the robot correct errors at bends. Failures are still off_track. The s-bend finishes 1 of 20 and the slalom 0 of 20, with progress only 0.20 and 2 line-loss events per run. Max_error still reaches the 0.06 m limit on the slalom, so the failures are excursions at sharp direction changes, not drift. Oval finish time is about 2.1 s, so there is speed margin for the oval but little for the slalom. Changes: (1) mass 0.5 to 0.45 kg, continuing the direction that clearly helped (yaw inertia falls by about 10 percent). (2) base_speed 1.25 to 1.15, to reduce lateral demand and bend-entry speed on tight sections, mainly the slalom. The oval will slow by roughly 8 percent (about 2.3 s, still under 3 s). Sensors, kp, kd, ki and line_loss are kept, because iteration 2 showed that changing sensor footprint or span made things worse. Expected result: oval finish rate of 0.75 or better, slalom progress above 0.3, and s-bend finishes rising. Hypotheses: (a) the slalom failure comes from entry speed, so a lower base_speed should cut its off_track events; (b) mass keeps helping, so yaw inertia is still a limit; (c) if slalom line_loss_events stay at 2, the 12 mm sensors are missing the tape at sharp bends, and a sensor-geometry test is needed next. Measurements wanted next: completion, progress, completion_time, max_error, line_loss_events and steering_oscillation on each track, plus control_effort to check steering load.
